correctness.rationale: The discrete infinite-horizon Gramian entries are geometric series. With \(x=\cos^2\theta\), its trace is affine in \(x\) and its determinant is \((pq-r^2)x(1-x)\), with \(pq-r^2>0\) exactly because the two stable eigenvalues are distinct. For a positive \(2\times2\) matrix, minimizing spectral condition number is equivalent to minimizing trace squared over determinant. That scalar quotient has the unique global minimizer \(x=q/(p+q)\), since it diverges at both endpoints. Substitution equalizes the diagonal entries and gives eigenvalue ratio \((1+\rho)/(1-\rho)\). The hyperbolic identity and coalescence asymptotic follow exactly. The packaged checker independently replays an exact rational example.

originality.rationale: Gramian-based actuator placement, condition-number use as a controllability quality measure, and the diagonalizable-system Hadamard formula are prior work. The closest full paper on Hadamard Gramian actuator selection was inspected through its discrete-time construction and single-input optimization section; it optimizes determinant, trace inverse, and trace and contains no located condition-number statement. Earlier condition-number work studies network-size/topology scaling rather than continuous actuator-direction optimization. Targeted published-record and exact-form searches did not locate the optimal direction or the hyperbolic-separation law.
residual_risks: Older modal-control or optimal-actuator literature may contain the same two-state condition-number minimization under different terminology.
Condition number is coordinate-sensitive outside orthonormal modal coordinates, so broader normal/nonnormal formulations can differ materially.
The condition-number objective is less common than determinant, trace inverse, and smallest-eigenvalue metrics, which can make exact prior art harder to retrieve by terminology.

value.rationale: Gramian eigenvalues quantify easy and hard control directions, so their ratio is a natural scale-free anisotropy measure. The theorem solves the smallest nontrivial continuous actuator-design problem exactly: it identifies the direction that balances modal control energies, distinguishes that direction from the standard determinant optimum, and shows that nearly coincident stable modes impose an unavoidable quadratic conditioning penalty on every scalar actuator orientation. This gives a compact structural diagnostic for actuator-direction design rather than a routine recomputation.
